You are Fa, a coding agent (also called fa). Never refer to yourself as pi, Claude, or any other assistant name. You help with software engineering tasks in the working directory /home/runner/work/flutter_agent_harness/flutter_agent_harness. Use the read, write, ls, and bash tools to inspect and modify files and run commands. Be concise.

## Agent messaging

You have an inbox in the session-shared messaging fabric. Your address is `01a124a3-d98e-717e-a450-adf777e022e4/main`. Other Fa instances running in this project have their own inboxes — their orchestrators are reachable at `<theirSessionId>/main`, your subagents at their plain ids. Live instances also expose their session display name (`--session goal_builder`): `agent_directory` shows it next to the mailbox id, and `agent_message` accepts the name directly — `goal_builder` or `goal_builder/main` — so you rarely need the raw id. Use the `agent_directory` tool to list the live mailboxes (plus anything holding pending mail; pass `all: true` for long-dead ones and full mailbox ids — the default view truncates ids to save tokens) and `agent_message` to send. Each row also shows the last-activity time: `active 2m ago` means the watcher is live, `last active 3h ago (asleep)` means the process is gone. If you message an asleep target, the harness automatically launches a detached headless run of its session (`fa --session <name>`) to process the inbox; that run appends to the same session JSONL, so a later interactive start resumes the same conversation. Incoming mail is delivered to you automatically between turns (and wakes you when idle); reply with `agent_message` to the sender's address when a response is expected. Never guess mailbox addresses — read them from `agent_directory`.
When a hub is configured, `agent_directory` also lists hub peers beyond this project's file inboxes (embedded hosts, other machines) with their id and name — message them with `agent_message` the same way; the hub delivers even while a peer is offline (it drains when the peer reconnects).

Peers on OTHER machines are addressed `name@machine` (use a machine name you were told, or one from the peer itself): `agent_message to: "goal_builder@renderbox"` routes through the A2A gateway when this host's config has an `a2a.servers.renderbox` entry — delivery is synchronous there, so an error means the mail did NOT land (retry or tell the user). Without that config entry the send fails with the exact hint of what to add.

## The owner talks to you only

The owner's messages always arrive in YOUR inbox — subagents and children are your internal machinery, never the owner's address. Decide per message: answer directly when you know, or route it to the child doing that work with `task_send` and tell the owner you did (e.g. «передал fix503»); when the child's result lands, report it back. While children run you may go idle — the waiting row names them, and completions and new mail wake you.

tools.name: read
tools.description:
Read the contents of a text file or image. Text output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large text files. Images are returned as base64 content.

## Path selectors

Append a trailing selector to `path` to read exactly the lines you need:

- `:N` — start at line N (1-indexed), through end of file. `:N-` is the same.
- `:A-B` — inclusive line range (`:A..B` works too).
- `:A+C` — C lines starting at A.
- `:R1,R2,…` — multiple ranges, sorted and merged (`:5-16,960-973`); blocks are joined with a `…` separator and ranges past end of file are reported as skipped.
- `:raw` — verbatim content: no line numbers, no hashline header, no notices. Combine as `:raw:50-100` or `:50-100:raw`.

Do not combine `offset`/`limit` with a path selector. Selectors only apply to text files (not images).

## Archives

Read inside `.zip`, `.tar`, `.tar.gz`/`.tgz` files: `archive.zip` lists the root, `archive.zip:dir/` lists a directory, `archive.zip:inner/file.txt` reads a member (selectors apply, e.g. `archive.zip:inner/file.txt:50-60`). Binary members return a note.

## SQLite databases

When the host supports it, `.db`/`.db3`/`.sqlite`/`.sqlite3` paths read as databases: `data.db` lists tables, `data.db:table` shows the schema plus sample rows, `data.db:table:key` fetches one row by primary key (or rowid), `data.db:table?limit=20&offset=40&order=col:desc&where=...` pages a table, and `data.db?q=SELECT ...` runs a raw read-only query.

## Hashline mode

Set hashline=true to prefix lines with line numbers and a [path#TAG] content-hash header for anchoring hashline edit patches (line numbers stay correct on ranged reads). Suppressed by `:raw`.

tools.name: write
tools.description: Write content to a file, creating parent directories as needed. Overwrites the file if it already exists.

tools.name: edit
tools.description:
Edit a file in one of two modes.

## Exact-match mode: `path` + `oldText` + `newText`

Replace an exact text occurrence. `oldText` must match exactly (including indentation and newlines) and occur exactly once in the file. Prefer this over `write` for small, precise changes to existing files; read the file first to get the exact text.

## Hashline mode: `patch`

A hashline patch names lines to replace, delete, or insert at by number, bound to a `[PATH#TAG]` content-hash header — precise line addressing without re-quoting file text. To author one, first `read` the file with `hashline=true`: it returns a `[PATH#TAG]` header and `LINE:TEXT` rows. Rule of thumb: a header ending in `:` is followed by `+` body rows; `DEL` has no body.

<headers>
Every file section starts with `[PATH#TAG]`. `TAG` = the 4-hex snapshot tag from your latest hashline `read` or edit response, REQUIRED on every section. Create new files with `write`; hashline only edits existing files. One patch may carry several `[PATH#TAG]` sections (different files); all sections apply or none do.
</headers>

<ops>
`SWAP N.=M:` — replace original lines N.=M with the body rows below. INCLUSIVE — line M is consumed too.
`DEL N.=M` — delete original lines N.=M. No body.
`INS.PRE N:` — insert the body rows immediately before line N.
`INS.POST N:` — insert the body rows immediately after line N.
`INS.HEAD:` / `INS.TAIL:` — insert the body rows at the very start / end of the file.
Single line: `SWAP N.=N:` / `DEL N`. The range is the ORIGINAL lines you touch; body length is irrelevant (replacing 1 line with 10 is still `SWAP N.=N:`).
</ops>

<body-rows>
Body rows appear only under a `:` header. Every body row is `+TEXT` — add a literal line `TEXT`, verbatim (leading whitespace kept); `+` alone adds a blank line. No other row kind. NEVER write `-old` or a bare/context line. To keep a line, leave it out of every range. Literal lines starting with `-`/`+` still need the body prefix: Markdown `- item` → `+- item`, `+ item` → `++ item`.
</body-rows>

<rules>
- Line numbers + `[PATH#TAG]` header come from your latest hashline `read` (`LINE:TEXT` rows) or edit response.
- Numbers refer to the ORIGINAL file; never shift as hunks apply.
- They die with the call: every applied edit mints a fresh `#TAG` and renumbers — anchor the next edit on the edit response or a fresh hashline `read`.
- Touch only lines your latest `read` literally displayed as `LINE:TEXT`; the tag certifies the snapshot, not your memory. A hunk anchored on a line you never displayed is REJECTED — re-`read` that range first.
- Never start or end a range mid-expression or mid-block.
- Indent body rows exactly for the depth they should live at.
- On a stale-tag rejection or any surprising result: STOP and re-`read` before further edits.
- One hunk per range; body = final content, never an old/new pair.
- Ranges cover ONLY lines whose content changes. Never widen over unchanged lines — a stale wide range shreds everything it spans.
- Pure additions use `INS.PRE` / `INS.POST` / `INS.HEAD` / `INS.TAIL`, never a widened `SWAP`.
- Non-adjacent changes = separate hunks; untouched lines stay out of every range.
- NEVER format/restyle code with this tool; run the project formatter instead.
</rules>

<example>
Original (the exact shape `read` with `hashline=true` returns):
```
[greet.py#A1B2]
1:def greet(name):
2:    msg = "Hello, " + name
3:    print(msg)
4:greet("world")
```

Insert a guard after line 1:
```
[greet.py#A1B2]
INS.POST 1:
+    if not name: name = "stranger"
```

Replace line 2 with two lines:
```
[greet.py#A1B2]
SWAP 2.=2:
+    greeting = "Hi"
+    msg = f"{greeting}, {name}"
```

Delete line 3:
```
[greet.py#A1B2]
DEL 3
```

Add a header and trailer:
```
[greet.py#A1B2]
INS.HEAD:
+# generated header
INS.TAIL:
+greet("everyone")
```

Insert Markdown bullets — the leading `+` is the body-row marker; the file receives `- task`:
```
[PLAN.md#A1B2]
INS.POST 2:
+- task
+  - nested task
```
</example>

<anti-patterns>
# WRONG — `-` rows / bare context lines do not exist. The range deletes; the body is only the new content.
SWAP 3.=3:
    msg = "Hello, " + name
-   print(msg)
+   return msg
# RIGHT
SWAP 3.=3:
+   return msg

# WRONG — a pure insertion done as a widened `SWAP`: you want to add one line after 2,
# but you replace 2.=4, retype the keepers, and risk dropping one.
SWAP 2.=4:
+    msg = "Hello, " + name
+    extra = compute(name)
+    print(msg)
# RIGHT — touch nothing you keep; the new line is the whole body.
INS.POST 2:
+    extra = compute(name)
</anti-patterns>

<critical>
If you remember nothing else:
1. RE-GROUND AFTER EVERY EDIT. Every apply mints a fresh `#TAG` and renumbers — take the next edit's numbers from the edit response or a fresh hashline `read`. Stale tag or surprise? STOP, re-`read`.
2. RANGES ARE TIGHT. Cover only lines that change; a stale wide range shreds everything it spans.
3. THE BODY IS THE FINAL CONTENT. Every body row starts with `+`; Markdown bullets use `+- item`, not `- item`.
</critical>

tools.name: ls
tools.description: List directory contents. Returns entries sorted alphabetically, with '/' suffix for directories. Output is truncated to 500 entries or 50KB (whichever is hit first).

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to the last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Optionally provide a timeout in seconds. Timeout-class failures are retried automatically (3 attempts total) — a hung network call does not fail the call; retries are visible as [bash attempt N] notices in the output. For long-running commands (builds, servers, watchers) pass background: true — the command keeps running as a job, you get its id immediately and are notified when it finishes; check progress with bash_job. A foreground command that is still running when the user sends a message is moved to a background job untouched (never killed) so the user gets an answer right away.

tools.name: bash_job
tools.description: Manage background shell jobs (from bash background: true). Actions: "status" lists running + last 20 exited (all: true = every job; id = one), "output" tails a log (id, lines), "stop" kills a running job (id).

tools.name: lsp
tools.description:
Query a language server for diagnostics, navigation, and renames. For Dart/Flutter workspaces the Dart analysis server (`dart language-server`) starts automatically on first use; other servers can be added via `.fah/lsp.json`.

## Ops

- `diagnostics {path}` — analyzer errors/warnings for a file. Returns `OK` when clean.
- `definition {path, line, character}` — where the symbol at the position is defined.
- `references {path, line, character}` — every reference to the symbol at the position.
- `rename {path, line, character, newName}` — rename the symbol at the position workspace-wide. The server's workspace edit is applied atomically, so barrel files and imports update together; per-file edit counts are reported.

`line` and `character` are 1-indexed and default to 1.

## Rules

- Prefer this over `bash dart analyze` for a single file; diagnostics come back scoped and severity-sorted.
- Prefer `rename` over manual search-and-replace for identifiers: the analysis server finds every reference, including exports and imports.
- Positions point at the symbol's first letter. When unsure of the exact column, `read` the line first.
- Definition/references results render as `file:line:col` with the source line; follow up with `read` for more context.
- If no server is configured for a file type, add one to `.fah/lsp.json` (servers map with `command`, `args`, `fileTypes`, `rootMarkers`).

tools.name: web_search
tools.description: Search the web and return ranked results with [n] citation markers, titles, URLs, and snippets. Runs a provider chain (DuckDuckGo first, keyed providers when configured) and falls through on failure. Follow up with web_fetch on a result URL to read the full page.

tools.name: web_fetch
tools.description: Fetch a web page and return its main content as Markdown: headings, link anchors, lists, and code blocks are preserved, navigation and boilerplate are stripped. Known sites (pub.dev) are rendered via dedicated handlers. Use it to read pages found with web_search.

tools.name: config
tools.description: Inspect and edit the fa configuration — the user file ~/.fah/config.yaml and the project .fah/config.yaml — without a shell (the same core the `fa config` CLI verbs wrap, available on every host). ops: check = validate both files with the real parsers (errors/warnings/notes + a final ok/failed line); path = list the config file locations and whether each exists; get = the effective value of a dotted key (project scope wins where it participates); set = a surgical single-key write that validates the edited file BEFORE writing, so an invalid value persists nothing. Config keys are documented in the fa-self-config skill — never invent one; unknown keys are rejected. A set result names the file, scope, old -> new value, and whether the change applies live or at next boot.

tools.name: memory_add
tools.description:
# `memory_add` policy

## What to store

Store only **durable** facts — things that must survive across sessions:

- project conventions, architecture decisions and their rationale;
- user preferences, habits, environment facts;
- key discoveries that were expensive to learn (non-obvious behaviour,
  gotchas, working configurations).

Do **not** store task progress, transient state, or anything derivable
from the repository itself (file contents, git history, current diffs).

## The supersede rule

Facts age. When a problem is **solved** or a fact **changes**:

1. delete the outdated record (`memory_delete` by id or exact text —
   deletions are tombstoned, so the old text cannot be re-captured);
2. add the new fact as a fresh record.

Never leave temporary difficulties, workarounds, or "currently broken"
notes in memory forever. A memory full of solved problems actively
misleads future sessions. If you used a record to fix something, that
record's job is done — supersede it.

Before adding anything, `memory_search` for an existing record on the
topic: update (delete + add) instead of duplicating.

## Scope discipline

- **project scope** (default) lives in the project's memory directory and
  is **public**: it is committed to git and shared with everyone who
  clones the repository. Never store secrets, credentials, personal data,
  or anything you would not put in a public commit message.
- **user scope** is global and private to the user's machine. Use it for
  cross-project preferences and facts about the user.

## Style

- One fact per record, concise and self-contained (readable without the
  conversation that produced it).
- Add concrete tags (see [tag_taxonomy.md](tag_taxonomy.md)).
- Prefer facts with staying power: "tests run with `--exclude-tags
  integration`" outlives "I am currently fixing the test suite".

tools.name: memory_search
tools.description: Search long-term memory for relevant facts, preferences, or past decisions. Use proactively before tasks that might benefit from prior context.

tools.name: memory_list
tools.description: List recent long-term memory entries. Useful to review what the agent already knows.

tools.name: memory_delete
tools.description: Delete a stale, wrong, or obsolete entry from long-term memory by id. Prefer deleting over rewriting when the fact no longer holds at all.

tools.name: schedule_message
tools.description: Send a delayed message to an agent mailbox (your own by default) — schedule a follow-up task to check on something later. The message wakes the recipient when it fires; it survives restarts.

tools.name: ask
tools.description:
Ask the user one or more structured questions when you need clarification or a decision during task execution.

<conditions>
- Multiple approaches exist with significantly different tradeoffs the user should weigh
</conditions>

<instruction>
- Use `questions` for multiple related questions instead of asking one at a time
- Use `recommended` (0-based option index or exact option label) to mark the default; the UI badges it as "Recommended"
- Set `multiSelect: true` on a question to allow multiple selections
- Use short option labels; put explanatory tradeoffs in an option's `description` instead of merging them into the label
- Omit `options` when the answer is free-form text
</instruction>

<caution>
- Provide 2-5 concise, distinct options per question
</caution>

<critical>
- **Default to action.** Resolve ambiguity yourself using repo conventions, existing patterns, and reasonable defaults. Exhaust existing sources (code, configs, docs, history) before asking. Only ask when options have materially different tradeoffs the user must decide.
- **If multiple choices are acceptable**, pick the most conservative/standard option and proceed; state the choice.
- **Do NOT include an "Other" option** — the UI always offers free-text input alongside your options.
</critical>

tools.name: request_secret
tools.description:
Ask the user for a credential (API key, token, password) that you need and that is not available yet.

<conditions>
- A command or call fails because a credential is missing, or the task clearly requires one
- The secret is NOT already in the "Available secret env vars" list
</conditions>

<instruction>
- Set `name` to the conventional env var name for the service (GITHUB_TOKEN, OPENAI_API_KEY, NPM_TOKEN...); the user can adjust it before saving
- Explain in `reason` what you need the credential for — the user sees this text
- After the user saves it, reference it as $NAME in shell commands; the value itself never enters the conversation
</instruction>

<critical>
- NEVER ask the user to paste a secret into the chat as plain text — always use this tool, so the value is stored securely and redacted from the transcript
- NEVER print, echo, or write the secret value after it is saved
- If the user declines, do not immediately retry the same request; find another way or explain the blocker
</critical>

tools.name: generate_image
tools.description: Generates an image from a text prompt. Returns a path to the saved image file. Arguments: prompt (required), size (optional, e.g. "1024x1024"), quality (optional).

tools.name: generate_video
tools.description: Generates a video from a text prompt. Returns a path to the saved MP4 file. Arguments: prompt (required), size (optional, e.g. "1920x1080"), quality (optional).

tools.name: task_status
tools.description: Check the status of spawned subagents. Without an id, lists ALL subagents with their current state, token usage, and last activity. With an id, shows that subagent in detail.

tools.name: task_observe
tools.description: Read the recent message history of a subagent. Useful to inspect what a child discovered or decided before following up.

tools.name: task_send
tools.description: Send a follow-up message to a subagent. A running child receives it in its inbox at the next turn boundary; an idle (waiting for input) or completed child is resumed in its SAME session with the message. The resume wait is capped (1s): a child that does not respond in time reports the message queued and keeps waking in the background (check task_status). Failed children are continued with task_resume instead. Remote a2a:<name> children cannot be steered or resumed — they have no local session or inbox; follow up with a new task item.

tools.name: task_resume
tools.description: Resume a FAILED subagent, continuing the SAME session: the run appends to the existing JSONL transcript, keeps the same mailbox id and display name, and never mints a cloned "name-2" session. Use this after transient failures (provider quota, network). Steering running/idle/completed children is task_send; respawning a fresh agent is task (the new child links supersedes).

tools.name: task_cancel
tools.description: Abort a running background subagent job by id (see task_status for ids). The child agent is cancelled; already-settled jobs report their state instead.

tools.name: reply
tools.description: Deliver your explicit answer to the parent agent. Call this when your task output is ready — the text becomes the parent-visible reply. If you never call it, the parent still sees your final message as a completion notice, but an explicit reply is the reliable channel.

tools.name: agent_message
tools.description: Send a message to another agent: a SIBLING subagent id, "main" for the parent orchestrator (for a final answer prefer reply), an absolute mailbox "<sessionId>/main" to reach another Fa instance sharing this session repo, or "name@machine" to reach a session on another machine (delivered through the A2A gateway; the remote machine must be configured under a2a.servers). A session display NAME from agent_directory works too: "goal_builder" or "goal_builder/main" resolve to that session's live mailbox. The recipient sees the message in its inbox on its next turn; completed siblings are resumed. Unknown ids and full queues are rejected.

tools.name: agent_directory
tools.description: List the agent mailboxes in the messaging fabric that are worth talking to: LIVE mailboxes (registration-backed presence or recent activity), any mailbox holding pending mail, your subagents, and your own address (marked). Each entry shows its session display NAME when known, a short mailbox id, the pending message count, presence ("live" / "busy (run in progress, accepts mail)" / "offline"), the last-activity time for offline entries, and the working directory (home shortened to ~). Declared capabilities render as sub-lines. Stale mailboxes are hidden — pass all: true to list those too (that also shows FULL mailbox ids; the default view truncates them to save tokens). Address a mailbox by its session name via agent_message ("goal_builder", "goal_builder/main", or "name@machine" — a peer on another machine is reachable through the A2A gateway when an a2a.servers entry exists for it); asleep targets are woken with a headless run automatically.

tools.name: task
tools.description:
Run subagents in parallel by passing multiple items in a single `tasks[]` batch. Execution blocks until every item finishes unless `background` is true — then you receive job ids immediately and results deliver as jobs settle.

# Task Design
- **Agent typing:** Pick each item's `agent` type. Read-only research MUST use `agent: "explore"`. Use the default worker only when no specialist fits.
- **No overhead:** Each `task` MUST instruct its subagent to skip formatters, linters, and project-wide test suites. Run those once at the end.
- **One pass:** Prefer subagents that investigate AND edit in one pass; spin a read-only `explore` only when the affected files are genuinely unknown.

# Inputs
- `context`: Shared project state, constraints, and contracts. Applies to the entire batch; do not duplicate this background into individual tasks.
- `tasks[]`: Array of subagents to spawn.
  - `name`: A stable identifier (`[A-Za-z0-9_-]`), used to address the agent (`agent://` urls, job ids). Uniquified per session; generated from the agent type if omitted.
  - `agent`: The agent type running this item. Omitting it gives you the general-purpose worker (`task`) — NEVER pass that name explicitly. Only omit it after checking the agent list below and finding no specialist that fits.
  - `task`: Complete, self-contained instructions. One-liners or missing acceptance criteria are PROHIBITED.
  - `outputSchema`: Invocation-specific JSON Schema. The subagent's final message must then be a JSON document satisfying it; invalid output gets ONE fix retry, then the item fails.
- `background`: Run items as background jobs (default: host configuration). Blocking calls return every item's output in the result.

# Communication
Subagents start blank — no conversation history. Put everything they need into `context` (shared) and `task` (per item). After spawn, the family stays connected:
- `task_send {id, message}`: steer a running child, answer a waiting (idle) one, or RESUME a completed one with follow-up work.
- `task_resume {id, message?}`: continue a FAILED child in its SAME session — same id, same transcript, same mailbox, never a cloned `name-2` session. Use it after transient failures (provider quota, network); `task_send` is for running/idle/completed children, a fresh `task` for a clean restart (the new child links `supersedes`).
- `task_status` / `task_observe`: inspect the family at any time — status, tokens, and the child's recent transcript.
- Children can `reply` (their explicit answer to you) and `agent_message` (sibling↔sibling hand-offs) — a child that finishes without replying surfaces a `completed_without_reply` notice with its final text preview.
- Completed subagents stay addressable: send them more work instead of re-spawning duplicates.
- Remote `a2a:<name>` children cannot be steered, resumed, or observed — they have no local session. Follow up with a new task item against the same `a2a:<name>` agent.

# Waiting is idle, not blocked
- Long-running children (test suites, builds, research): spawn them with `background: true` and END YOUR TURN right after spawning. Completions and inbox mail wake you automatically, and each result arrives as a message — waiting is an idle state, never a blocked turn.
- NEVER park your turn waiting on children (foreground watch loops, blocking re-polls, sleep-style watchers). A parked turn is unreachable: owner messages queue behind it for as long as the wedge lasts.
- If a blocking call is still running when a user message arrives, the call soft-yields to background — do not re-block afterwards; finish the reply and end the turn.

# Format Contracts
`context` format:
# Goal         ← what the batch accomplishes
# Constraints  ← rules and session decisions
# Contract     ← shared interfaces

`task` format:
# Target       ← exact files and symbols; explicit non-goals
# Change       ← step-by-step add/remove/rename; APIs and patterns
# Acceptance   ← observable result; no project-wide commands

# Results
Each item's full output is addressable as `agent://<id>`. For items with an `outputSchema`, the stored output IS the validated JSON object, so typed fields are addressable as `agent://<id>/<dot.path>` (e.g. `agent://Explore/findings.0.path`).

# Available Agents
### task
General-purpose subagent with full capabilities for delegated multi-step tasks
### explore (READ-ONLY)
Read-only codebase research: rapid analysis, pattern searches, and compressed findings for handoff (uses the smol model role when configured)
### review (READ-ONLY)
Read-only code review specialist for quality and security analysis (uses the slow model role when configured)
### plan (READ-ONLY)
Read-only planning specialist that produces implementation plans without editing code

tools.name: checkpoint
tools.description:
Creates a context checkpoint before exploratory work so you can later rewind and keep only a concise report.

Use this when you need to investigate with many intermediate tool calls (read/grep/glob/etc.) and want to minimize context cost afterward.

Rules:
- You MUST call `rewind` before finishing after starting a checkpoint.
- You NEVER call `checkpoint` while another checkpoint is active in the
  same turn. A checkpoint never spans user turns: if one is left unrewound
  when the turn ends, the next `checkpoint` call auto-closes it (the tool
  result names the closed checkpoint) and proceeds.

Typical flow:
1. `checkpoint(goal: …)`
2. Perform exploratory work
3. `rewind(report: …)` with concise findings

After rewind, intermediate checkpoint messages are removed from active context and replaced by the report. The dropped history stays in the session tree; nothing is lost.

tools.name: rewind
tools.description:
End an active checkpoint. Rewind context to it, replacing intermediate exploration with your report.

Call immediately after `checkpoint`-started investigative work.

Requirements:
- `report` MUST be concise, factual, and actionable.
- Include key findings, decisions, and any unresolved risks.
- AVOID raw scratch logs unless essential.
- You MUST call this before finishing if a checkpoint is active.

Behavior:
- If no checkpoint is active, this tool errors. If the checkpoint already rewound, continue from the retained report instead of retrying.
- On success, the session rewinds, keeps your report as retained context, and closes the checkpoint.
- A successful rewind is final for that checkpoint; repeat calls error.

tools.name: compact_expand
tools.description:
Surface and reopen hidden context segments.

Call with NO arguments to list what is hidden: the index of hidden segments with id, kind, size, and a first-line preview each. Pass `query` to filter and rank that index by keyword — it searches the full hidden content, not just previews, so use it when you know WHAT you need but not the id. Discovery is free: it never consumes the expand budget.

To read a segment back, pass its numeric id or range from a marker as `target` (e.g. `5` or `2-6`). Context markers like `[3:hidden·tool_result·4.2k·"first line…"]` or `[2-6:ckpt·38k→40tok·covers:3,5]` are doors, not gravestones: the underlying records stay on disk.

- Giant segments are paged: pass `page` (1-based) to continue past the first page; each page footer states the exact continue call.
- Expanded content counts toward a per-turn budget; every success states the budget left, and when the budget is exhausted the result says so and resets on the next user turn. Only hidden, checkpoint-covered, or summary-folded records expand — the tool tells you when a record is already visible.
- The session file never changes; an expanded segment may be re-hidden later by compaction.

Prefer a targeted expand over re-reading files when the fact was already in context once, and prefer discovery + query over blind ids.

## Managing segments yourself (tier 2)

Pass `action` with a `target` to manage segments directly, without waiting for pressure:

- `action: "hide"` folds a segment you know is dead weight into its expandable marker immediately — one-line marker stays where the content was, `compact_expand` reopens it any time. Real user turns are never hideable; pair groups hide whole; the most recent turns and pinned segments are rejected with the reason.
- `action: "pin"` shields a segment from every hide/compact path (yours, the judge's, pressure-time LRU re-hide); `action: "unpin"` releases it. Pins render on the marker (`·pinned`) and survive session reload.

Hiding and pinning are session state, not edits: the records stay in the file byte-for-byte.

{"content":"🚨 **BLOCKING: the custom path's `FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG` is rejected by the Dart env preconfig — every custom trial dies at container boot**

The custom arm builds the shard config with a verbatim passthrough plus the fixed key-env injection (line 280):

```bash
provider_config=$(printf '%s' "$PROVIDER_CONFIG" | jq -c --arg k "$key_env" '. + {apiKeyEnvVar: $k}')
```

For the **documented** input shape (`provider-config: {"type","baseUrl","model","contextWindow","maxTokens"}`, per the input description and pinned by `test_custom_provider_config_flows_verbatim_with_fixed_key_env`), this produces:

```json
{"type":"openai","baseUrl":"https://api.example.com/v1","model":"m-1","contextWindow":128000,"maxTokens":8192,"apiKeyEnvVar":"FA_KEY_BENCH_CUSTOM"}
```

The Dart consumer does not accept a `type` key inside `FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG` — `_supportedConfigKeys` is `baseUrl, model, apiKeyEnvVar, contextWindow, maxTokens, input, thinkingLevel` only. Verified against this branch:

```
ConfigException: unknown FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG key: "type" — supported keys: baseUrl, model, apiKeyEnvVar, contextWindow, maxTokens, input, thinkingLevel
  package:flutter_agent_harness/src/cli/env_provider_preconfig.dart  _takeConfigEntry
```

And `faProviderPreconfig`'s contract is deliberate: *"a container that names its provider wrong must fail loud at boot"* — so a custom dispatch burns a whole shard of trials that all fail at fa boot. The run only works if the user **omits** `type` (then `.type // "openai"` sets `provider_type` with no `type` key in the JSON) — i.e. the opposite of the documented example.

Two sound fixes (pick one):

1. **Strip `type` in the passthrough** — it already rides the dedicated `FA_PROVIDER_TYPE` output/env:
   ```bash
   provider_config=$(printf '%s' "$PROVIDER_CONFIG" | jq -c --arg k "$key_env" 'del(.type) + {apiKeyEnvVar: $k}')
   ```
2. **Accept `type` Dart-side** — add it to `_supportedConfigKeys` and cross-check it equals the resolved `FA_PROVIDER_TYPE` (a mismatch would be a loud misconfiguration).

Either way, add one cross-layer test: feed the workflow resolve step's actual `provider_config` output into `parseEnvProviderPreconfig` (the two sides are currently pinned by separate tests with opposite expectations — which is exactly how this slipped through).

1. **baseUrl echoed in the https-check failure message**: `got: $(printf '%s' "$PROVIDER_CONFIG" | jq -r '.baseUrl')` — echoes baseUrl only, not the whole config. baseUrl is not secret. OK.

2. **The jq `words` regex**: `gsub("(?<l>[a-z0-9])(?<u>[A-Z])"; "\(.l)_\(.u)")` — splits camelCase. Then `gsub("[ _-]+"; ")`, downcase, split. Then tests each word against `^(api.?key|apikey|key|token|secret)$`. Note `api.?key` covers "api_key"→split to "api key"? Wait: "api_key" → gsub `[ _-]+` → "api key" → split → ["api","key"] → "key" matches. "apiKey" → "api_Key" → "api key" → ["api","key"] — "key" matches. Good. But what about a field named "apikey"? → ["apikey"] matches `apikey` and `api.?key`. Good. What about "monkey"? → ["monkey"] — `key` anchored with ^$ doesn't match "monkey". Good — whole-word avoids false positive... wait, "monkey" is one word, and the regex is `^key$`, no match. 

   Hmm, but what about a nested field value carrying a key? E.g. `{"baseUrl": "...", "model": "...", "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer sk-..."}}` — key-like field names are checked only at top level (`keys[]`). A custom provider config could legitimately need extra headers... but a key could be smuggled in a *value* of a benign-named field. No — env vars of a step aren't in run metadata; but the resolve step writes provider_config to GITHUB_OUTPUT, which is fine (values aren't secrets). The real risk per D1: the *dispatch input* is visible in run metadata. The validation prevents a user from *intentionally* putting key material in the input — the hard-fail on key-like field names covers the accidental case. A determined user could smuggle a key in any field value, but that's true of any system; the ticket's requirement is field-name detection. OK.

The custom arm builds the shard config with a verbatim passthrough plus the fixed key-env injection (line 280):

```bash
provider_config=$(printf '%s' "$PROVIDER_CONFIG" | jq -c --arg k "$key_env" '. + {apiKeyEnvVar: $k}')
```

For the **documented** input shape (`provider-config: {"type","baseUrl","model","contextWindow","maxTokens"}`, per the input description and pinned by `test_custom_provider_config_flows_verbatim_with_fixed_key_env`), this produces:

```json
{"type":"openai","baseUrl":"https://api.example.com/v1","model":"m-1","contextWindow":128000,"maxTokens":8192,"apiKeyEnvVar":"FA_KEY_BENCH_CUSTOM"}
```

The Dart consumer does not accept a `type` key inside `FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG` — `_supportedConfigKeys` is `baseUrl, model, apiKeyEnvVar, contextWindow, maxTokens, input, thinkingLevel` only. Verified against this branch:

```
ConfigException: unknown FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG key: "type" — supported keys: baseUrl, model, apiKeyEnvVar, contextWindow, maxTokens, input, thinkingLevel
  package:flutter_agent_harness/src/cli/env_provider_preconfig.dart  _takeConfigEntry
```

And `faProviderPreconfig`'s contract is deliberate: *"a container that names its provider wrong must fail loud at boot"* — so a custom dispatch burns a whole shard of trials that all fail at fa boot. The run only works if the user **omits** `type` (then `.type // "openai"` sets `provider_type` with no `type` key in the JSON) — i.e. the opposite of the documented example.

Two sound fixes (pick one):

1. **Strip `type` in the passthrough** — it already rides the dedicated `FA_PROVIDER_TYPE` output/env:
   ```bash
   provider_config=$(printf '%s' "$PROVIDER_CONFIG" | jq -c --arg k "$key_env" 'del(.type) + {apiKeyEnvVar: $k}')
   ```
2. **Accept `type` Dart-side** — add it to `_supportedConfigKeys` and cross-check it equals the resolved `FA_PROVIDER_TYPE` (a mismatch would be a loud misconfiguration).

Either way, add one cross-layer test: feed the workflow resolve step's actual `provider_config` output into `parseEnvProviderPreconfig` (the two sides are currently pinned by separate tests with opposite expectations — which is exactly how this slipped through).

## PR Description

Closes #1471
## What changed

The terminal-bench workflow stops hardcoding the z.ai GLM provider: a new `provider` dispatch choice (`zai-glm-5.3-flash` default / `kimi-for-coding`) is resolved in the setup job to the full provider triple and preflighted against the selected bench secret before any shard starts; kimi runs on a dedicated `FA_BENCH_KIMI_KEY` (never `KIMI_REVIEW_KEY`) as `kimi` / `api.kimi.com/coding/v1` / `k3-256k`. The `FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG` env contract now accepts optional `contextWindow`/`maxTokens` (rides the resolver's override layer into the booted model), and the run identity (workflow `run-name`, shard job names via `needs` outputs, summary `Provider:` header via `BENCH_RUN_LABEL`) names provider+model. `bench/pricing.json` gains an explicit zero entry for `k3-256k` with a comment (subscription plan, no published per-token price — never an invented number).

## Key decisions

- Resolve + secret preflight live in the **setup job** (presence check only, key value never echoed; base64 form masked like the shard step's standing contract) — a bad dispatch fails in minute one, burning zero shard-hours; shard jobs consume the resolved outputs via `needs`.
- REG-1: the default choice resolves the exact legacy 3-field zai JSON (`model` still sourced from the `BENCH_MODEL` pin) — pinned byte-for-byte by a UT.
- Shard step maps **both** bench secrets and the run block picks the resolved key by name (`${!FA_PROVIDER_KEY_ENV}`) — no dynamic `secrets[...]` indexing, block stays env-driven and testable by the existing shell-harness family.
- `contextWindow: 200000` / `maxTokens: 16384` are declared explicitly for kimi (matches the catalog spec today, but immune to catalog drift); undeclared zai boots stay byte-identical.
- Artifact names (`tb-runs-shard-N`) intentionally unchanged — the merge job downloads by that pattern; run identity rides `run-name`/job name/summary header.

## How to verify

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s bench/terminal_bench   # 328 tests, incl. new ProviderResolveStepTest + shape tests
dart test test/cli/env_provider_preconfig_test.dart test/model_roles/provider_catalog_test.dart
actionlint .github/workflows/bench.yml                  # clean

The custom implementation looks thorough. Let me scrutinize the security-sensitive bits:

1. **baseUrl echoed in the https-check failure message**: `got: $(printf '%s' "$PROVIDER_CONFIG" | jq -r '.baseUrl')` — echoes baseUrl only, not the whole config. baseUrl is not secret. OK.

2. **The jq `words` regex**: `gsub("(?<l>[a-z0-9])(?<u>[A-Z])"; "\(.l)_\(.u)")` — splits camelCase. Then `gsub("[ _-]+"; ")`, downcase, split. Then tests each word against `^(api.?key|apikey|key|token|secret)$`. Note `api.?key` covers "api_key"→split to "api key"? Wait: "api_key" → gsub `[ _-]+` → "api key" → split → ["api","key"] → "key" matches. "apiKey" → "api_Key" → "api key" → ["api","key"] — "key" matches. Good. But what about a field named "apikey"? → ["apikey"] matches `apikey` and `api.?key`. Good. What about "monkey"? → ["monkey"] — `key` anchored with ^$ doesn't match "monkey". Good — whole-word avoids false positive... wait, "monkey" is one word, and the regex is `^key$`, no match. 

   Hmm, but what about a nested field value carrying a key? E.g. `{"baseUrl": "...", "model": "...", "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer sk-..."}}` — key-like field names are checked only at top level (`keys[]`). A custom provider config could legitimately need extra headers... but a key could be smuggled in a *value* of a benign-named field. However, the config JSON flows verbatim into FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG which is NOT a secret — it lands in the shard env and into fa_agent.py, and from there into the container env as FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG_BASE64... Actually wait, is FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG visible in run metadata? No — env vars of a step aren't in run metadata; but the resolve step writes provider_config to GITHUB_OUTPUT, which is fine (values aren't secrets). The real risk per D1: the *dispatch input* is visible in run metadata. The validation prevents a user from *intentionally* putting key material in the input — the hard-fail on key-like field names covers the accidental case. A determined user could smuggle a key in any field value, but that's true of any system; the ticket's requirement is field-name detection. OK.

   But wait — one more: what about key-like fields NESTED in objects, e.g. `{"options": {"apiKey": "[REDACTED:credential]"}}`? `keys[]` only checks top-level. The ticket says "any field named like apiKey/key/token/secret" — arguably top-level is what was specified. jq `keys` on the root object. Nested would be more thorough but the ticket's language is satisfied. Could note as SUGGESTION. Hmm, exhaustive review... a nested key field would ride verbatim into FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG — but FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG is not a secret input; it's the workflow output. The leak concern is run metadata visibility of dispatch inputs. If a nested key field exists, the key value sits in the dispatch input → visible in run metadata → leaked. But again, a user can put a key in ANY value. The D1 protection is best-effort against accidental pasting of a well-formed config including an apiKey field. I'll consider mentioning nested scanning as a SUGGESTION... Let me think about whether it's worth it. The standard config generators produce flat JSON. The ticket example is flat. I'd rate it a minor SUGGESTION at most; maybe skip to avoid noise. Actually the exhaustive-pass instruction says surface all actionable findings. A one-line jq change (`.. | objects | keys[]`) would do it. I'll include as SUGGESTION.

3. **`provider_type` from custom**: `jq -r '.type // "openai"'`. But hold on — FA_PROVIDER_TYPE consumed by Dart's parseEnvProviderPreconfig: unknown provider type throws ConfigException. If a user passes `type: "kimi"` in provider-config, the Dart side resolves it against the catalog — kimi is a catalog entry, so fine. If they pass an unknown type, the container boot fails loudly. Ticket D1: "type optional (default openai-compatible)". OK.

   But one subtlety: `type` value could be non-string, e.g. `{"type": 123}` → `jq -r` prints "123" → provider_type="123" → shard env FA_PROVIDER_TYPE=123 → Dart parse fails loud in container. Acceptable (fails loud). Could validate string — SUGGESTION-level at most. Also `.model` non-string: the required-field check above ensures `type == "string" and length > 0` for model. But between the check and the `jq -r '.model'` re-parse, same value. OK.

   What if `.type` is present but empty string `""`? `// "openai"` — jq `//` treats false and null as absent, but "" is truthy in jq! `"" // "openai"` → `""` in jq? Actually in jq, `//` operator: `a // b` produces `a` if `a` is neither false nor null. Empty string IS produced. So provider_type="" → FA_PROVIDER_TYPE empty → Dart: providerType empty string → parseEnvProviderPreconfig treats... Let me check: `required String? providerType` — empty string might be treated as absent (the preconfig parse typically treats blank as absent). If absent → falls back to anthropic default in fa_agent (`os.environ.get("FA_PROVIDER_TYPE", "anthropic")` — but env var IS set, to ""). Dart parseEnvProviderPreconfig: let me check how it handles empty providerType. Probably `providerType?.trim().isEmpty` → null → no preconfig → agent boots with default provider (anthropic, no key) → loud failure in container. Edge case, user error, fails loud. Minor. Not worth a finding? The resolve step could validate `type` when present: non-empty string. I'll bundle into a suggestion about validating `.type` (string, non-empty) — maybe combined with the nested-key suggestion? Separate concerns; keep separate comments if I include both. Let me not over-produce; I'll flag the `type` validation as one SUGGESTION.

4. **jq availability**: ubuntu-latest runners have jq preinstalled. The shard step uses jq? The resolve step now depends on jq being present on the runner. GHA ubuntu images include jq. Existing workflow — does it already use jq anywhere? Let me grep. If the repo avoids jq elsewhere, that's a new tool dependency, but it's standard on GHA runners. Fine.

5. **fa_agent.py docstring** — check the +7 lines.

6. **env_provider_preconfig.dart refactor** — check _takeConfigEntry and CRAP.

7. **test_summary_1392.py** — 2-line change (label spelling).

8. Verify tests run: 336 python UTs claimed. Run them.

9. **PROVIDER_CONFIG env in resolve step**: `PROVIDER_CONFIG: ${{ inputs.provider-config }}` — the input is interpolated into the step env. Env values aren't echoed. The failure messages don't echo the raw input. But wait — GitHub Actions prints the resolved env block? No, it doesn't print env values. OK.

   One consideration: step env with a multi-line JSON input — inputs can contain newlines? workflow_dispatch text inputs are single-line. JSON single line. OK.

10. **provider_config output for custom** — `jq -c '. + {apiKeyEnvVar: $k}'` — compact, single line. Written to GITHUB_OUTPUT. Contains baseUrl/model but no key. OK.

11. **run_label for custom**: `custom ($model)` — model from user input could contain weird chars (e.g. `)` or newline)? model is validated as a string; could contain `$(...)`? It's used in job names via needs outputs — GHA renders as data, not shell. Fine. Could contain unicode. Fine.

12. **CRITICAL re-check — the shard run block indirection**: FA_PROVIDER_KEY_ENV now can be FA_KEY_BENCH_CUSTOM, and the shard env maps FA_KEY_BENCH_CUSTOM from secrets.FA_BENCH_CUSTOM_KEY. Both resolve step (setup) and shard map it. Good.

13. Check that `FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG` for custom with `contextWindow`/`maxTokens` passes through verbatim — yes, jq -c '. + {apiKeyEnvVar}' keeps all fields. And Dart parse handles them. Good — AC 2a + D4 compose.

14. Check the **secret preflight for custom**: `secret_value=$FA_BENCH_CUSTOM_KEY` — under set -u, env var is always defined in the env block. Good; missing secret → empty → error names FA_BENCH_CUSTOM_KEY. AC 3 ✓.

# Pull Request Information

- **PR #**: 1475
- **URL**: https://github.com/IstiN/flutter_agent_harness/pull/1475
- **Title**: gh-1471 [GOAL] bench.yml: provider selection for tbench runs (zai-glm default, kimi-for-coding) with a dedicated bench key
- **Author**: ai-teammate
- **Branch**: `ai/gh-1471` → `main`
- **State**: open
- **Files Changed**: 12
- **Additions**: +1221
- **Deletions**: -55
- **Created**: 2026-10-10T06:51:24Z
- **Updated**: 2026-10-10T08:46:30Z

## PR Description

Closes #1471
## What changed

The terminal-bench workflow stops hardcoding the z.ai GLM provider: a new `provider` dispatch choice (`zai-glm-5.3-flash` default / `kimi-for-coding`) is resolved in the setup job to the full provider triple and preflighted against the selected bench secret before any shard starts; kimi runs on a dedicated `FA_BENCH_KIMI_KEY` (never `KIMI_REVIEW_KEY`) as `kimi` / `api.kimi.com/coding/v1` / `k3-256k`. The `FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG` env contract now accepts optional `contextWindow`/`maxTokens` (rides the resolver's override layer into the booted model), and the run identity (workflow `run-name`, shard job names via `needs` outputs, summary `Provider:` header via `BENCH_RUN_LABEL`) names provider+model. `bench/pricing.json` gains an explicit zero entry for `k3-256k` with a comment (subscription plan, no published per-token price — never an invented number).

## Key decisions

- Resolve + secret preflight live in the **setup job** (presence check only, key value never echoed; base64 form masked like the shard step's standing contract) — a bad dispatch fails in minute one, burning zero shard-hours; shard jobs consume the resolved outputs via `needs`.
- REG-1: the default choice resolves the exact legacy 3-field zai JSON (`model` still sourced from the `BENCH_MODEL` pin) — pinned byte-for-byte by a UT.
- Shard step maps **both** bench secrets and the run block picks the resolved key by name (`${!FA_PROVIDER_KEY_ENV}`) — no dynamic `secrets[...]` indexing, block stays env-driven and testable by the existing shell-harness family.
- `contextWindow: 200000` / `maxTokens: 16384` are declared explicitly for kimi (matches the catalog spec today, but immune to catalog drift); undeclared zai boots stay byte-identical.
- Artifact names (`tb-runs-shard-N`) intentionally unchanged — the merge job downloads by that pattern; run identity rides `run-name`/job name/summary header.

## How to verify

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s bench/terminal_bench   # 328 tests, incl. new ProviderResolveStepTest + shape tests
dart test test/cli/env_provider_preconfig_test.dart test/model_roles/provider_catalog_test.dart
actionlint .github/workflows/bench.yml                  # clean
```

Owner setup (E2E blocker, not the code): add the repo secret `FA_BENCH_KIMI_KEY`, then smoke `tasks=hello-world, provider=kimi-for-coding, 1 shard`.

Note: `dart test test/cli/` (full dir) passes all 245 tests but the VM aborts in glibc at process shutdown on this runner — reproduced identically on clean `origin/main` (pre-existing environment issue, unrelated to this change).

<details>
<summary>Architecture diagram</summary>

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  DISP[workflow_dispatch provider choice] --> RES[setup: Resolve provider]
  SEC1[secrets.FA_BENCH_ZAI_KEY] --> RES
  SEC2[secrets.FA_BENCH_KIMI_KEY] --> RES
  RES -->|unknown choice / missing secret: [REDACTED:Sensitive Value] fail, zero shard-hours| X1((fail))
  RES -->|outputs: type, config JSON, key env, run_label| SHARD[bench shard jobs]
  SHARD -->|FA_PROVIDER_TYPE / FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG / key by name| AG[fa_agent.py → container env preconfig]
  AG --> MODEL[buildCliDefaultModel: declared contextWindow/maxTokens win]
  SHARD --> SUM[summary.py: Provider: run_label + pinned MODEL]
```

</details>

# Pull Request Information

- **PR #**: 1475
- **URL**: https://github.com/IstiN/flutter_agent_harness/pull/1475
- **Title**: gh-1471 [GOAL] bench.yml: provider selection for tbench runs (zai-glm default, kimi-for-coding) with a dedicated bench key
- **Author**: ai-teammate

- **Deletions**: -55

- **Updated**: 2026-10-10T08:46:30Z

## PR Description

Closes #1471
## What changed

The terminal-bench workflow stops hardcoding the z.ai GLM provider: a new `provider` dispatch choice (`zai-glm-5.3-flash` default / `kimi-for-coding`) is resolved in the setup job to the full provider triple and preflighted against the selected bench secret before any shard starts; kimi runs on a dedicated `FA_BENCH_KIMI_KEY` (never `KIMI_REVIEW_KEY`) as `kimi` / `api.kimi.com/coding/v1` / `k3-256k`. The `FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG` env contract now accepts optional `contextWindow`/`maxTokens` (rides the resolver's override layer into the booted model), and the run identity (workflow `run-name`, shard job names via `needs` outputs, summary `Provider:` header via `BENCH_RUN_LABEL`) names provider+model. `bench/pricing.json` gains an explicit zero entry for `k3-256k` with a comment (subscription plan, no published per-token price — never an invented number).

## Key decisions

- Resolve + secret preflight live in the **setup job** (presence check only, key value never echoed; base64 form masked like the shard step's standing contract) — a bad dispatch fails in minute one, burning zero shard-hours; shard jobs consume the resolved outputs via `needs`.
- REG-1: the default choice resolves the exact legacy 3-field zai JSON (`model` still sourced from the `BENCH_MODEL` pin) — pinned byte-for-byte by a UT.
- Shard step maps **both** bench secrets and the run block picks the resolved key by name (`${!FA_PROVIDER_KEY_ENV}`) — no dynamic `secrets[...]` indexing, block stays env-driven and testable by the existing shell-harness family.
- `contextWindow: 200000` / `maxTokens: 16384` are declared explicitly for kimi (matches the catalog spec today, but immune to catalog drift); undeclared zai boots stay byte-identical.
- Artifact names (`tb-runs-shard-N`) intentionally unchanged — the merge job downloads by that pattern; run identity rides `run-name`/job name/summary header.

## How to verify

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s bench/terminal_bench   # 328 tests, incl. new ProviderResolveStepTest + shape tests
dart test test/cli/env_provider_preconfig_test.dart test/model_roles/provider_catalog_test.dart
actionlint .github/workflows/bench.yml                  # clean
```

Owner setup (E2E blocker, not the code): add the repo secret `FA_BENCH_KIMI_KEY`, then smoke `tasks=hello-world, provider=kimi-for-coding, 1 shard`.

Note: `dart test test/cli/` (full dir) passes all 245 tests but the VM aborts in glibc at process shutdown on this runner — reproduced identically on clean `origin/main` (pre-existing environment issue, unrelated to this change).

<details>
<summary>Architecture diagram</summary>

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  DISP[workflow_dispatch provider choice] --> RES[setup: Resolve provider]
  SEC1[secrets.FA_BENCH_ZAI_KEY] --> RES
  SEC2[secrets.FA_BENCH_KIMI_KEY] --> RES
  RES -->|unknown choice / missing secret: [REDACTED:Sensitive Value] fail, zero shard-hours| X1((fail))
  RES -->|outputs: type, config JSON, key env, run_label| SHARD[bench shard jobs]
  SHARD -->|FA_PROVIDER_TYPE / FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG / key by name| AG[fa_agent.py → container env preconfig]
  AG --> MODEL[buildCliDefaultModel: declared contextWindow/maxTokens win]
  SHARD --> SUM[summary.py: Provider: run_label + pinned MODEL]
```

</details>

- **PR #**: 1475
- **URL**: https://github.com/IstiN/flutter_agent_harness/pull/1475
- **Title**: gh-1471 [GOAL] bench.yml: provider selection for tbench runs (zai-glm default, kimi-for-coding) with a dedicated bench key
- **Author**: ai-teammate

- **Updated**: 2026-10-10T08:46:30Z

## PR Description

Closes #1471
## What changed

The terminal-bench workflow stops hardcoding the z.ai GLM provider: a new `provider` dispatch choice (`zai-glm-5.3-flash` default / `kimi-for-coding`) is resolved in the setup job to the full provider triple and preflighted against the selected bench secret before any shard starts; kimi runs on a dedicated `FA_BENCH_KIMI_KEY` (never `KIMI_REVIEW_KEY`) as `kimi` / `api.kimi.com/coding/v1` / `k3-256k`. The `FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG` env contract now accepts optional `contextWindow`/`maxTokens` (rides the resolver's override layer into the booted model), and the run identity (workflow `run-name`, shard job names via `needs` outputs, summary `Provider:` header via `BENCH_RUN_LABEL`) names provider+model. `bench/pricing.json` gains an explicit zero entry for `k3-256k` with a comment (subscription plan, no published per-token price — never an invented number).

## Key decisions

- Resolve + secret preflight live in the **setup job** (presence check only, key value never echoed; base64 form masked like the shard step's standing contract) — a bad dispatch fails in minute one, burning zero shard-hours; shard jobs consume the resolved outputs via `needs`.
- REG-1: the default choice resolves the exact legacy 3-field zai JSON (`model` still sourced from the `BENCH_MODEL` pin) — pinned byte-for-byte by a UT.
- Shard step maps **both** bench secrets and the run block picks the resolved key by name (`${!FA_PROVIDER_KEY_ENV}`) — no dynamic `secrets[...]` indexing, block stays env-driven and testable by the existing shell-harness family.
- `contextWindow: 200000` / `maxTokens: 16384` are declared explicitly for kimi (matches the catalog spec today, but immune to catalog drift); undeclared zai boots stay byte-identical.
- Artifact names (`tb-runs-shard-N`) intentionally unchanged — the merge job downloads by that pattern; run identity rides `run-name`/job name/summary header.

## How to verify

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s bench/terminal_bench   # 328 tests, incl. new ProviderResolveStepTest + shape tests
dart test test/cli/env_provider_preconfig_test.dart test/model_roles/provider_catalog_test.dart
actionlint .github/workflows/bench.yml                  # clean
```

Owner setup (E2E blocker, not the code): add the repo secret `FA_BENCH_KIMI_KEY`, then smoke `tasks=hello-world, provider=kimi-for-coding, 1 shard`.

Note: `dart test test/cli/` (full dir) passes all 245 tests but the VM aborts in glibc at process shutdown on this runner — reproduced identically on clean `origin/main` (pre-existing environment issue, unrelated to this change).

<summary>Architecture diagram</summary>

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  DISP[workflow_dispatch provider choice] --> RES[setup: Resolve provider]
  SEC1[secrets.FA_BENCH_ZAI_KEY] --> RES
  SEC2[secrets.FA_BENCH_KIMI_KEY] --> RES
  RES -->|unknown choice / missing secret: [REDACTED:Sensitive Value] fail, zero shard-hours| X1((fail))
  RES -->|outputs: type, config JSON, key env, run_label| SHARD[bench shard jobs]
  SHARD -->|FA_PROVIDER_TYPE / FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG / key by name| AG[fa_agent.py → container env preconfig]
  AG --> MODEL[buildCliDefaultModel: declared contextWindow/maxTokens win]
  SHARD --> SUM[summary.py: Provider: run_label + pinned MODEL]
```

</details>

But now consider: the whitelist check below only checks TOP-LEVEL keys (`[. | keys[] ...]`) — nested unknown keys are NOT rejected by the whitelist (only scanned for key-like names). A nested object like `{"options": {...}}` — top-level key "options" is not in the whitelist → rejected. Good: top-level whitelist is closed, so arbitrary nesting is impossible except through whitelisted keys, none of which are objects (contextWindow etc. are scalars; input is a list of strings). So nested objects can only appear... they can't, since top-level non-whitelisted keys are rejected. Wait — but the key-like scan runs BEFORE the whitelist check. Nested objects can exist in the INPUT at scan time (e.g. {"headers": {"apiKey": "[REDACTED:credential]"}}), and the scan catches the nested apiKey. Then whitelist rejects "headers". Both good. Actually the nested scan is now belt-and-braces since whitelist blocks all object-valued top-level keys... but input could be checked as array of strings. OK.

     | $v == null or (($v | type) == "string" and ($v | test("^\\s*$")))

The custom arm builds the shard config with a verbatim passthrough plus the fixed key-env injection (line 280):

```bash
provider_config=$(printf '%s' "$PROVIDER_CONFIG" | jq -c --arg k "$key_env" '. + {apiKeyEnvVar: $k}')
```

For the **documented** input shape (`provider-config: {"type","baseUrl","model","contextWindow","maxTokens"}`, per the input description and pinned by `test_custom_provider_config_flows_verbatim_with_fixed_key_env`), this produces:

```json
{"type":"openai","baseUrl":"https://api.example.com/v1","model":"m-1","contextWindow":128000,"maxTokens":8192,"apiKeyEnvVar":"FA_KEY_BENCH_CUSTOM"}
```

The Dart consumer does not accept a `type` key inside `FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG` — `_supportedConfigKeys` is `baseUrl, model, apiKeyEnvVar, contextWindow, maxTokens, input, thinkingLevel` only. Verified against this branch:

```
ConfigException: unknown FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG key: "type" — supported keys: baseUrl, model, apiKeyEnvVar, contextWindow, maxTokens, input, thinkingLevel
  package:flutter_agent_harness/src/cli/env_provider_preconfig.dart  _takeConfigEntry
```

And `faProviderPreconfig`'s contract is deliberate: *"a container that names its provider wrong must fail loud at boot"* — so a custom dispatch burns a whole shard of trials that all fail at fa boot. The run only works if the user **omits** `type` (then `.type // "openai"` sets `provider_type` with no `type` key in the JSON) — i.e. the opposite of the documented example.

Two sound fixes (pick one):

1. **Strip `type` in the passthrough** — it already rides the dedicated `FA_PROVIDER_TYPE` output/env:
   ```bash
   provider_config=$(printf '%s' "$PROVIDER_CONFIG" | jq -c --arg k "$key_env" 'del(.type) + {apiKeyEnvVar: $k}')
   ```
2. **Accept `type` Dart-side** — add it to `_supportedConfigKeys` and cross-check it equals the resolved `FA_PROVIDER_TYPE` (a mismatch would be a loud misconfiguration).

Either way, add one cross-layer test: feed the workflow resolve step's actual `provider_config` output into `parseEnvProviderPreconfig` (the two sides are currently pinned by separate tests with opposite expectations — which is exactly how this slipped through).

# Pull Request Information

- **PR #**: 1475
- **URL**: https://github.com/IstiN/flutter_agent_harness/pull/1475
- **Title**: gh-1471 [GOAL] bench.yml: provider selection for tbench runs (zai-glm default, kimi-for-coding) with a dedicated bench key
- **Author**: ai-teammate
- **Branch**: `ai/gh-1471` → `main`
- **State**: open
- **Files Changed**: 12
- **Additions**: +1221
- **Deletions**: -55
- **Created**: 2026-10-10T06:51:24Z
- **Updated**: 2026-10-10T08:46:30Z

## PR Description

Closes #1471
## What changed

The terminal-bench workflow stops hardcoding the z.ai GLM provider: a new `provider` dispatch choice (`zai-glm-5.3-flash` default / `kimi-for-coding`) is resolved in the setup job to the full provider triple and preflighted against the selected bench secret before any shard starts; kimi runs on a dedicated `FA_BENCH_KIMI_KEY` (never `KIMI_REVIEW_KEY`) as `kimi` / `api.kimi.com/coding/v1` / `k3-256k`. The `FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG` env contract now accepts optional `contextWindow`/`maxTokens` (rides the resolver's override layer into the booted model), and the run identity (workflow `run-name`, shard job names via `needs` outputs, summary `Provider:` header via `BENCH_RUN_LABEL`) names provider+model. `bench/pricing.json` gains an explicit zero entry for `k3-256k` with a comment (subscription plan, no published per-token price — never an invented number).

## Key decisions

- Resolve + secret preflight live in the **setup job** (presence check only, key value never echoed; base64 form masked like the shard step's standing contract) — a bad dispatch fails in minute one, burning zero shard-hours; shard jobs consume the resolved outputs via `needs`.
- REG-1: the default choice resolves the exact legacy 3-field zai JSON (`model` still sourced from the `BENCH_MODEL` pin) — pinned byte-for-byte by a UT.
- Shard step maps **both** bench secrets and the run block picks the resolved key by name (`${!FA_PROVIDER_KEY_ENV}`) — no dynamic `secrets[...]` indexing, block stays env-driven and testable by the existing shell-harness family.
- `contextWindow: 200000` / `maxTokens: 16384` are declared explicitly for kimi (matches the catalog spec today, but immune to catalog drift); undeclared zai boots stay byte-identical.
- Artifact names (`tb-runs-shard-N`) intentionally unchanged — the merge job downloads by that pattern; run identity rides `run-name`/job name/summary header.

## How to verify

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s bench/terminal_bench   # 328 tests, incl. new ProviderResolveStepTest + shape tests
dart test test/cli/env_provider_preconfig_test.dart test/model_roles/provider_catalog_test.dart
actionlint .github/workflows/bench.yml                  # clean
```

Owner setup (E2E blocker, not the code): add the repo secret `FA_BENCH_KIMI_KEY`, then smoke `tasks=hello-world, provider=kimi-for-coding, 1 shard`.

Note: `dart test test/cli/` (full dir) passes all 245 tests but the VM aborts in glibc at process shutdown on this runner — reproduced identically on clean `origin/main` (pre-existing environment issue, unrelated to this change).

<details>
<summary>Architecture diagram</summary>

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  DISP[workflow_dispatch provider choice] --> RES[setup: Resolve provider]
  SEC1[secrets.FA_BENCH_ZAI_KEY] --> RES
  SEC2[secrets.FA_BENCH_KIMI_KEY] --> RES
  RES -->|unknown choice / missing secret: [REDACTED:Sensitive Value] fail, zero shard-hours| X1((fail))
  RES -->|outputs: type, config JSON, key env, run_label| SHARD[bench shard jobs]
  SHARD -->|FA_PROVIDER_TYPE / FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG / key by name| AG[fa_agent.py → container env preconfig]
  AG --> MODEL[buildCliDefaultModel: declared contextWindow/maxTokens win]
  SHARD --> SUM[summary.py: Provider: run_label + pinned MODEL]
```

</details>

The rework since fa721496d (my last review) touched: bench.yml (+92), test_bench_workflow.py (+186), scripts/test_quarantine.json (+12 — hmm, that's odd; probably from a main merge), env_provider_preconfig_test.dart (+49).

blocks.text:
The rework addresses my blocking finding: `del(.type)` before emission + capability blank-drop + a whole family of preflight checks mirroring the Dart consumer, plus a cross-layer Dart test pinning the consumer side. The test_quarantine.json change came from the main merge (not this PR's own change — it came via origin/main merge commit #1470). Wait, actually it's in the PR diff vs main? Since the branch merged origin/main into itself, the diff origin/main...HEAD wouldn't include it. The fa721..HEAD diff includes it because it came from main. Let me confirm: `git diff origin/main...HEAD -- scripts/test_quarantine.json` should be empty.

Now I must re-review the new jq validation logic carefully for bugs. Let me analyze each check:

1. **apiKeyEnvVar rejection** — good; prevents silent override.

2. **Nested key-like scan**: `[.. | objects | keys[] | ...]` with `unique` — descends nested. But now consider: the whitelist check below only checks TOP-LEVEL keys (`[. | keys[] ...]`) — nested unknown keys are NOT rejected by the whitelist (only scanned for key-like names). A nested object like `{"options": {...}}` — top-level key "options" is not in the whitelist → rejected. Good: top-level whitelist is closed, so arbitrary nesting is impossible except through whitelisted keys, none of which are objects (contextWindow etc. are scalars; input is a list of strings). So nested objects can only appear... they can't, since top-level non-whitelisted keys are rejected. Wait — but the key-like scan runs BEFORE the whitelist check. Nested objects can exist in the INPUT at scan time (e.g. {"headers": {"apiKey": "[REDACTED:credential]"}}), and the scan catches the nested apiKey. Then whitelist rejects "headers". Both good. Actually the nested scan is now belt-and-braces since whitelist blocks all object-valued top-level keys... but input could be checked as array of strings. OK.

3. **Whitelist check**: keys allowed: baseUrl, model, contextWindow, maxTokens, input, thinkingLevel, type. Note it excludes "apiKeyEnvVar" deliberately (checked separately above with a clearer message). Good. Error message says "supported keys: baseUrl, model, contextWindow, maxTokens, input, thinkingLevel (type selects FA_PROVIDER_TYPE...)" — accurate.

4. **type check**: `if has("type") and .type != null then (.type | type == "string" and test("\\S")) else true end`. Note: `has("type")` true with null value → else branch → true (treated absent). Dart side: `"type"` is stripped anyway, so a null type is fine. OK.

5. **capability check** `capok(min)`:
   ```jq
   def capok(min): . as $v
     | $v == null or (($v | type) == "string" and ($v | test("^\\s*$")))
     or (($v | type) == "number" and ($v | floor) == $v and $v >= min);
   (.contextWindow | capok(16384)) and (.maxTokens | capok(1024))
   ```
   
   Analysis:
   - `$v == null` → absent OK.
   - string all-blank → absent OK (Dart treats blank string as absent — confirmed in _parseCapabilityInt: `if (value is String && value.trim().isEmpty) return null;`). And the emission step deletes blank capability fields. ✓ consistent.
   - number, integer (floor == self), >= min OK.
   
   BUT: what about a blank string with whitespace like " — test("^\\s*$") matches → treated absent. Emission `del(.contextWindow | select(. == null or ((. | type) == "string" and (. | test("^\\s*$")))` deletes it. Dart would also treat as absent. Consistent. ✓
   
   What about a NON-blank string, e.g. "2000"? capok: not null, not blank-string, not number → false → error. Dart _parseCapabilityInt: non-blank string → `value is! int` → throws. Consistent. ✓
   
   Floor values: minOverrideContextWindow = 16384 ✓ (grep showed 49: `const int minOverrideContextWindow = 16384;`). minOverrideMaxTokens = minAnswerTokens — claimed 1024. Need to verify minAnswerTokens == 1024.

   jq `floor` on a number: works. For huge integers > 2^53, precision issues — irrelevant here.

   Edge: `.contextWindow | capok(...)` — if .contextWindow is a BOLEAN (true)? `$v == null` false; type=="string" false; type=="number" false → false → error. Dart: `value is! int` → throws. Consistent. ✓
   
   Edge: what about `contextWindow: 16384.0` in JSON? jsonDecode in jq: 16384.0 → number, floor == self → passes. Dart jsonDecode("16384.0") → double → `is! int` → THROWS. Inconsistent! A JSON `16384.0` passes preflight but fails Dart-side. Hmm — does jq parse 16384.0 as number with floor == 16384 == 16384.0? Yes passes. Dart: double 16384.0, `value is! int` true → ConfigException. So `.0`-suffixed floats pass preflight, die at boot. Edge-of-edge case (nobody writes 16384.0), and it fails loud at boot not silently wrong. Could be nit-picked but... jq cannot distinguish 16384 from 16384.0 after parsing (both numbers). Actually jq CAN: `tostring` — 16384.0 tostring gives "16384"? Hmm, jq normalizes. There is no reliable way in jq to detect the textual ".0". So this is a jq limitation, unfixable cheaply; the failure remains loud at boot. Not worth flagging beyond maybe a mention. I'll skip — it's truly negligible and unfixable in jq.

6. **input check**: `type == "array" and length > 0 and all(.[]; . == "text" or . == "image")`. Dart _parseInputList: "a non-empty JSON array whose entries are exactly text/image". Consistent. But emission: `input` rides verbatim — Dart validates again anyway; consistent. ✓ Note jq `all(.[]; cond)` — correct syntax: `all(generator; condition)`. ✓

7. **thinkingLevel check**: string blank → absent OK; else in [minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, max]. Dart _parseThinkingLevel — the comment says "xhigh/max fold to high Dart-side". Need to verify the Dart ladder accepts exactly these values. Let me check _parseThinkingLevel / configThinkingLevels.

8. **Emission jq**:
   ```jq
   del(.type)
   | del(.contextWindow | select(. == null or ((. | type) == "string" and (. | test("^\\s*$")))
   | del(.maxTokens | select(. == null or ((. | type) == "string" and (. | test("^\\s*$")))
   | . + {apiKeyEnvVar: $k}
   ```
   `del(.contextWindow | select(...))` — deletes .contextWindow when the select matches. Correct jq idiom? `del(path | select(cond))` — yes, del accepts a path expression; if the select produces no matches, nothing deleted. ✓
   
   Wait, but if contextWindow is a blank string, the capok check treated it absent, and emission deletes it. Dart also absent. ✓. But NOTE: the thinkingLevel blank string is NOT dropped in emission — Dart treats blank thinkingLevel as absent? Check _parseThinkingLevel: blank → null presumably (comment says "a blank string is absent"). So passing `"thinkingLevel": "  "` through verbatim → Dart returns null. Fine.

9. **provider_type**: `jq -r '.type // "openai"'` — with validated non-empty string or absent. But note: if `.type` passed validation as a non-empty string with only whitespace? No — test("\\S") requires a non-whitespace char. ✓

10. **model**: `jq -r '.model'` — validated as non-empty string. Could contain newlines? JSON string with \n — a workflow_dispatch input is a single line, so can't contain a literal newline; could contain escaped sequences... whatever, it rides into job names — GHA sanitizes? Job name is display-only. Fine.

Now — did they also fix the Dart side or keep whitelist? They kept the Dart whitelist and strip type workflow-side. The cross-layer Dart test pins the consumer side for the documented example. 

One more check: the whitelist error message lists supported keys WITHOUT type but says "(type selects FA_PROVIDER_TYPE and is not echoed...)". OK.

Also verify: does the workflow UT family now cover the new preflight branches? test_bench_workflow.py +186 — let me check the new tests. Also re-run the suites. Also verify minAnswerTokens value and the thinkingLevel ladder in Dart.

Let me also confirm test_quarantine.json is NOT in the PR-vs-main diff (came via main merge).

messages.preview: Confirmed suspicion: the custom arm passes `"type"` through verbatim into `FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG`, but `_supportedConfigKeys` has no `type`. Let me prove the Dart side rejects the exact JSON the workflow…

blocks.text:
Confirmed: `_supportedConfigKeys` does NOT include `'type'`. And the custom arm passes `type` through verbatim. So a custom run with `"type":"openai"` in provider-config produces a FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG containing `"type":"openai"` → Dart `_takeConfigEntry` throws `ConfigException: unknown FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG key: "type"` → the preconfig fails → the container's fa boot fails for EVERY trial.

Wait — but I should double check how fa in the container consumes FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG. In bin/fah_runapp.dart, faPreconfig = parseEnvProviderPreconfig(...). If it throws ConfigException — is it caught or fatal? Let me check the call site. If it fails loud at boot, every task trial burns (the shard keeps running tasks that all fail). Either way: custom provider runs are broken for any config that includes `type` — and the input description + tests ENCOURAGE including type! The default when type is omitted: `.type // "openai"` — if the user omits type, then provider_config has no "type" key → Dart parse OK → works. So custom runs work only when type is omitted; the documented example `{"type","baseUrl","model","contextWindow","maxTokens"}` breaks.

Hold on — let me be very careful. `jq -c '. + {apiKeyEnvVar: $k}'` — keeps "type". Yes. ## PR Description

Closes #1471
## What changed

The terminal-bench workflow stops hardcoding the z.ai GLM provider: a new `provider` dispatch choice (`zai-glm-5.3-flash` default / `kimi-for-coding`) is resolved in the setup job to the full provider triple and preflighted against the selected bench secret before any shard starts; kimi runs on a dedicated `FA_BENCH_KIMI_KEY` (never `KIMI_REVIEW_KEY`) as `kimi` / `api.kimi.com/coding/v1` / `k3-256k`. The `FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG` env contract now accepts optional `contextWindow`/`maxTokens` (rides the resolver's override layer into the booted model), and the run identity (workflow `run-name`, shard job names via `needs` outputs, summary `Provider:` header via `BENCH_RUN_LABEL`) names provider+model. `bench/pricing.json` gains an explicit zero entry for `k3-256k` with a comment (subscription plan, no published per-token price — never an invented number).

## Key decisions

- Resolve + secret preflight live in the **setup job** (presence check only, key value never echoed; base64 form masked like the shard step's standing contract) — a bad dispatch fails in minute one, burning zero shard-hours; shard jobs consume the resolved outputs via `needs`.
- REG-1: the default choice resolves the exact legacy 3-field zai JSON (`model` still sourced from the `BENCH_MODEL` pin) — pinned byte-for-byte by a UT.
- Shard step maps **both** bench secrets and the run block picks the resolved key by name (`${!FA_PROVIDER_KEY_ENV}`) — no dynamic `secrets[...]` indexing, block stays env-driven and testable by the existing shell-harness family.
- `contextWindow: 200000` / `maxTokens: 16384` are declared explicitly for kimi (matches the catalog spec today, but immune to catalog drift); undeclared zai boots stay byte-identical.
- Artifact names (`tb-runs-shard-N`) intentionally unchanged — the merge job downloads by that pattern; run identity rides `run-name`/job name/summary header.

## How to verify

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s bench/terminal_bench   # 328 tests, incl. new ProviderResolveStepTest + shape tests
dart test test/cli/env_provider_preconfig_test.dart test/model_roles/provider_catalog_test.dart
actionlint .github/workflows/bench.yml                  # clean
```

Owner setup (E2E blocker, not the code): add the repo secret `FA_BENCH_KIMI_KEY`, then smoke `tasks=hello-world, provider=kimi-for-coding, 1 shard`.

Note: `dart test test/cli/` (full dir) passes all 245 tests but the VM aborts in glibc at process shutdown on this runner — reproduced identically on clean `origin/main` (pre-existing environment issue, unrelated to this change).

flowchart TD

  SEC1[secrets.FA_BENCH_ZAI_KEY] --> RES

  RES -->|outputs: type, config JSON, key env, run_label| SHARD[bench shard jobs]
  SHARD -->|FA_PROVIDER_TYPE / FA_PROVIDER_CONFIG / key by name| AG[fa_agent.py → container env preconfig]

+              # inside a header map rides through a top-level-only scan
